name: OpenSanctions (dataset)
purpose: Continuously built dataset of sanctioned entities, politically exposed persons, companies of interest and related entities, assembled from hundreds of official sources and published in FollowTheMoney format with the build pipeline open-sourced.
journalism_use_case: The screening layer for any investigation involving money or power: check a leaked client list, shareholder register or property dataset against sanctions and PEP data to find the names that matter. It is the difference between a spreadsheet of 40,000 names and a shortlist of twelve.
pros: Breadth and currency: hundreds of official source lists consolidated and rebuilt continuously, which no newsroom could replicate and which commercial screening vendors charge heavily for
Published in FollowTheMoney, so it joins directly to your own entity data through nomenklatura and yente without a mapping project
Code is MIT and the build pipeline is public (pushed 2026-11-17), so the provenance of every entity is traceable to its source list — which matters when a screening hit informs a published allegation
Self-hostable with yente, so screening happens on your infrastructure and your query targets stay private
cons: LICENCE BLOCKER for commercial use: the DATA is CC-BY-NC 4.0 and commercial use requires a paid licence, with the Screening Licence and Reseller/OEM options quote-only (verified on the vendor licensing page). A commercially operated newsroom cannot assume its use is non-commercial
PEP designation is a status, not an allegation: a match means a person holds or held public office or is connected to someone who does, and reporting it as suspicion would be wrong
Entity matching produces candidates requiring adjudication — name collisions are frequent, especially for common names in transliteration, so a hit is a question not a finding
No GitHub releases (continuous build), so pinning a dataset state for a reproducible analysis means recording the build date yourself
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The decisive documented facts: code licence MIT (licence blob read 2026-11-17, copyright OpenSanctions Datenbanken GmbH with earlier Friedrich Lindenberg and Journalism Development Network copyrights), and data CC-BY-NC 4.0 with commercial use requiring a paid licence and quote-only enterprise tiers (vendor licensing page, verified 2026-11-16). Recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md L6 and pricing.md.
assessment: Adopt the capability and settle the data licence explicitly in writing — that is the whole decision. Self-host with yente so query targets stay internal, and resolve whether your outlet's use is non-commercial before building a workflow on it; if it is not, price the commercial licence rather than relying on an optimistic reading of CC-BY-NC. Editorially, treat every match as a lead requiring identity confirmation, and never publish a PEP match as an implication of wrongdoing.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, no release objects (continuous build model), 878 stars, MIT code licence. Daily commits on the build pipeline with a commercial entity dependent on the dataset's currency — the strongest possible maintenance incentive.
model_or_data_licence: Data is CC-BY-NC 4.0; commercial use requires a paid licence (Screening Licence and Reseller/OEM are quote-only; the Screening API uses prepaid credit bundles with free credits on signup).
licence_restrictions: Material and the central consideration: NonCommercial bars commercial exploitation of the data, and NGO or journalism status does not automatically satisfy it. Publishing an article informed by the data is ordinary journalistic use; building a paid product or client-facing screening service on it is not. 'OpenSanctions is open source' is true of the code only.
costs: Code and non-commercial data use free. Commercial data licence: quote required, not publicly listed (verified 2026-11-16). Self-hosting needs an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch node for yente. Hosted Screening API sold in prepaid credit bundles. Estimate for self-hosting: one 8-16GB VM.
privacy: Self-hosting with yente keeps your screening queries entirely private — the decisive advantage over hosted screening APIs, which learn exactly whom you are investigating. The dataset itself concerns public figures and sanctioned entities.
alternatives: yente for the self-hosted screening API over this data
Official sanctions lists directly (OFAC, EU, UN) for a licence-free but far more laborious approach
Commercial screening vendors, which are expensive and disclose your query targets
blockers: Data is CC-BY-NC 4.0 — commercial-use licence required, price not publicly listed
summary: Continuously built dataset of sanctioned entities, politically exposed persons, companies of interest and related entities…
software_price_note: code free (MIT); the DATA is CC-BY-NC-4.0 — commercial use requires a paid licence, price not publicly listed (verified 2026-11-16)
additional_costs_note: mandatory paid data licence for commercial use (quote); optional hosted Screening API (prepaid credits); self-hosted Elasticsearch

name: Aleph (alephdata, original)
maintainer: OCCRP (original; development has moved to the OpenAleph fork)
purpose: Investigative data platform that indexes documents and structured datasets as FollowTheMoney entities, with search, cross-referencing between datasets and collaborative collections — the original OCCRP implementation.
journalism_use_case: The system that established this category and still runs OCCRP's own network. Catalogued here separately from OpenAleph because it is the repository most documentation, tutorials and search results point at, and because knowing which line is maintained is a concrete planning fact.
pros: The origin of the FollowTheMoney ecosystem and of entity-centric investigative search, so understanding it explains OpenAleph, yente, nomenklatura and much of the OSINT data tooling in this catalogue
MIT licensed with a substantial deployment history across investigative networks (2,513 stars)
OCCRP continues to operate Aleph for its own network, so the software works and is in production use
Documentation is more extensive than the fork's, reflecting years of deployment experience
cons: Maintenance of the public repository has visibly slowed: last push 2026-02-20 and latest release 4.1.7 (2025-10-27) — nine months without a push and over a year without a release, while the OpenAleph fork released 5.4.0 on 2026-11-16
No deprecation notice, which is the hazard: a newsroom following the documentation will deploy the less-maintained line without knowing a divergence exists
Heavy infrastructure (Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, Redis, ingest workers) for a version that is no longer the development focus
The ecosystem has moved: ingest-file's maintained fork is OpenAleph's, and FollowTheMoney's active line is OpenSanctions', so building on alephdata means assembling a stale stack
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The decisive documented facts, verified this session: alephdata/aleph archived=false, pushed 2026-02-20, release 4.1.7 (2025-10-27); openaleph/openaleph is a GitHub fork with parent=alephdata/aleph, pushed 2026-11-16, release 5.4.0 the same day. Recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md L3, and consistent with session 1's ground_truth.tsv note 'superseded by openaleph fork'.
assessment: Reference only — deploy OpenAleph instead. The reason this entry exists is that the divergence is invisible unless you check: alephdata/aleph is not archived, its documentation is better, and it is what search results surface, so a team acting reasonably will choose the wrong one. For your profile the single actionable fact is to point every link, bookmark and internal note at OpenAleph and the OpenSanctions FollowTheMoney line.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-02-20, latest release 4.1.7 (2025-10-27), 2,513 stars, 69 open issues on the related followthemoney repository. Nine months without a push and thirteen without a release, while the fork releases monthly. Declining rather than archived — and the absence of a deprecation notice is itself the risk.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Loaded datasets carry their own licences.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure equivalent to OpenAleph's (Elasticsearch cluster, PostgreSQL, Redis, workers) — a four-figure annual commitment plus ops time, which is not worth spending on the less-maintained line. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted with no required third-party calls, as with OpenAleph.
alternatives: OpenAleph — the maintained fork, use this instead
ICIJ Datashare for a document-centric alternative with lower operational burden
Hoover or Uwazi for lighter document-platform needs
blockers: Development has moved to the OpenAleph fork; no deprecation notice makes the stale line easy to adopt by mistake
summary: Investigative data platform that indexes documents and structured datasets as FollowTheMoney entities, with search…

name: Hoover
purpose: Search service for collections of documents and email archives, indexing text and metadata across heterogeneous sources with a search interface aimed at investigative use.
journalism_use_case: A lighter alternative to Aleph-class platforms for the common case: you have a document dump and a mailbox archive and you want reporters to search them together, without deploying an entity-resolution platform or operating an Elasticsearch cluster you do not need.
pros: Scoped deliberately to search rather than entity resolution, which makes it substantially lighter to deploy than OpenAleph for teams whose actual need is 'let reporters search these files'
Handles email archives alongside documents, which is the realistic composition of a leak and is awkward in general-purpose document systems
Built for investigative journalism by a project focused on that use case, so the interface assumptions match reporters rather than enterprise search
Repository path verified this session: hoover/search redirects to liquidinvestigations/hoover-search, so older references resolve
cons: Small project with limited community, so you will be reading source and the deployment documentation assumes familiarity with the stack
Multi-component architecture (search, snoop, UI) spread across repositories, which makes orientation slower than the scope suggests
Development cadence is modest, so it sits between 'maintained' and 'quiet' and warrants a liveness check before adoption
No entity extraction or cross-referencing, so if your investigation is entity-centric you will outgrow it and need OpenAleph anyway
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository transfer hoover/search → liquidinvestigations/hoover-search was confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17 (recorded in leads.md L4). Liquid Investigations' orientation to investigative journalism is documented by the project; I verified no specific newsroom deployment.
assessment: Worth evaluating if your need is genuinely search-only and OpenAleph's operational weight is the obstacle — which is a common and under-acknowledged situation. For your profile I would compare it against ICIJ Datashare in desktop mode first, since Datashare gives you search plus basic entity extraction with less deployment work and far stronger institutional backing. Choose Hoover if you need a server-side shared search over mixed documents and mail and want something lighter than Aleph.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with the organisation transfer confirmed. The project spans several repositories with modest activity and no clear release cadence, so maintenance cannot be confidently classified from metadata — hence Uncertain rather than an inferred classification in either direction. Check liveness directly before adopting.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; confirm the licence file before redistribution.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure: a multi-service deployment with a search index — lighter than OpenAleph but still a real deployment. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted; documents and mail stay on your infrastructure. The index is as sensitive as the collection and must not be exposed.
alternatives: ICIJ Datashare for search plus entity extraction with better support
OpenAleph where entity cross-referencing is needed
Apache Solr or OpenSearch plus a simple front end for a bespoke build
summary: Search service for collections of documents and email archives, indexing text and metadata across heterogeneous sources with a…

name: Overview
purpose: Document-analysis platform that clusters a document set by topic, provides tagging and full-text search, and presents a tree view so a reporter can explore a large collection by theme rather than one file at a time.
journalism_use_case: The original answer to 'I have ten thousand documents and three days': Overview clusters them into a navigable topic tree so a reporter can see the shape of the collection and read the interesting branches, which remains the right first move on an unfamiliar dump.
pros: Topic-tree navigation is genuinely reporter-friendly — it answers 'what is in here' without requiring the reporter to know what to search for, which keyword search cannot do
Built specifically for journalism by people who had watched reporters fail at document review, and the design shows it
AGPL-3.0 (licence verified in session 1 by reading the text, resolving a NOASSERTION), with a long history and a sizeable repository
Tagging and search alongside clustering means the exploration leads somewhere actionable
cons: Maintenance has clearly slowed, which is the dominant consideration: this is a mature platform whose active development period has passed, and deploying it means accepting that
Scala and multi-service architecture make self-hosting a substantial undertaking relative to the capability — BERTopic plus Datasette achieves comparable exploration with components you already run
Clustering quality is dated relative to current embedding-based topic modelling, so the topic tree is cruder than what BERTopic would produce today
The hosted Overview service's status and terms were not verified in this survey
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: session 1's a1disc/notes.md independently recorded 'overview-server AGPL-3.0' after reading the licence text, resolving a GitHub NOASSERTION. The project's journalism lineage is well documented; its reduced development pace is evident from the repository.
assessment: Reference only for new deployments, but the idea remains correct and worth reproducing: cluster first, then read. For your profile the modern equivalent is BERTopic for clustering plus Datasette or Datashare for search and tagging — components that are actively maintained and that you may already run. Overview's historical importance is that it established document clustering as a newsroom practice, and that practice is what to carry forward.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, but with substantially reduced development activity and no current release cadence. Session 1 verified the AGPL-3.0 licence by reading the text. Declining rather than dormant; no deprecation notice.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (verified in session 1 by reading the licence text, resolving a GitHub NOASSERTION)
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered to users obliges source publication.
costs: No software fee. Self-hosting a Scala multi-service platform is a meaningful operational commitment for the capability delivered. Hosted service terms not verified. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted keeps documents internal. The hosted service would place them with the operator — terms unverified.
alternatives: BERTopic plus Datasette for the same clustering-then-reading workflow with maintained components
ICIJ Datashare for search, tagging and entity extraction in a maintained platform
txtai for semantic exploration of a document set
blockers: Development pace has declined; the architecture is heavy relative to modern alternatives
summary: Document-analysis platform that clusters a document set by topic, provides tagging and full-text search…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: Uwazi
purpose: Document and entity management platform built for human-rights documentation, with customisable entity templates, relationships, multilingual interfaces, full-text search and public or private publishing.
journalism_use_case: Building a structured, publishable collection of documents and entities around a long-running investigation: court filings linked to defendants linked to incidents, with a custom data model, in several languages, publishable as a public resource when the reporting is done.
pros: Customisable entity templates and relationships mean you model your investigation's actual structure rather than fitting it to someone else's schema — a real advantage over fixed-model platforms
Built by a human-rights documentation organisation, so multilingual support, evidence handling and the private-to-public publishing transition are designed in rather than retrofitted
MIT licensed with exceptional maintenance: release 1.229.312 on 2026-11-16 and same-day pushes, independently recorded in session 1's ground_truth.tsv
Serves both the working-collection and the published-resource purposes, so a long investigation's archive becomes its public legacy without a migration
cons: Operational commitment: a Node and MongoDB application with Elasticsearch for search, so it is a platform to run rather than a tool to install
Flexibility is double-edged — a badly designed entity model is hard to change later, so the modelling decision at the start matters more than with a fixed-schema system
Oriented to curated collections rather than bulk leak triage: it is for the documents you have decided matter, not for the first pass over 500,000 files
Smaller community than the big document platforms, though with strong institutional backing
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: release 1.229.312 (2026-11-16) with same-day push, MIT licence — independently recorded in session 1's ground_truth.tsv as MIT, active, with the same release line. HURIDOCS deploys Uwazi with human-rights organisations, which is documented by the organisation.
assessment: Adopt it for long-running structured investigations, particularly where the output should become a public resource — that combination is what Uwazi does better than anything else here. For your profile the decisive design step is the entity model: spend real time on it before loading data, because the schema encodes your investigative questions. Keep bulk triage elsewhere (Datashare, OpenAleph) and move the documents that matter into Uwazi.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17 and session 1's independent check: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 1.229.312 (2026-11-16), MIT. Same-day release and push with a very high release count indicating continuous delivery, under institutional maintenance by HURIDOCS.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: Node application, MongoDB and Elasticsearch — one well-provisioned VM for a moderate collection, more as it grows. HURIDOCS offers hosting and support services (prices not verified). Assumptions: self-hosted, curated collection scale.
privacy: Self-hosted with private collections by default and an explicit publishing step, which is the right model for material that starts sensitive and becomes public. Residual risk is ordinary platform security.
alternatives: ICIJ Datashare for bulk document triage before curation
OpenAleph where cross-dataset entity resolution matters more than custom modelling
DocumentCloud for publishing documents without the entity layer
summary: Document and entity management platform built for human-rights documentation, with customisable entity templates, relationships…

name: Tella
purpose: Mobile application for documenting human-rights violations and collecting evidence in hostile environments, with encrypted local storage, camouflage modes, metadata capture and secure upload to a server or Uwazi instance.
journalism_use_case: Field documentation where the phone may be searched: a stringer records an incident, the file is encrypted on the device and the app can be camouflaged to look like a calculator, with upload to your server when connectivity and safety allow. This is the tool for the moment between witnessing and publishing.
pros: Camouflage and encrypted-at-rest storage address the specific threat field documenters face — a device search at a checkpoint — which no general camera or cloud app does
Uploads to infrastructure you control, including a Uwazi instance, so evidence moves from the field into your collection without passing through a commercial cloud
Captures verification-relevant metadata at the point of recording, strengthening the evidentiary value of material gathered under pressure
Built by an organisation focused on human-rights documentation, with the threat model stated explicitly
cons: Camouflage is a usability trade-off and a risk in itself: a trained searcher who knows Tella exists may find it, and a false sense of safety is dangerous — this must be explained honestly to users
Android focus, so an iOS-using contributor is less well served
Requires the documenter to install an app that, if identified, is itself incriminating in some jurisdictions — the same dilemma as Orbot and Tails
Depends on you operating a receiving server (or a Uwazi instance), so it is part of a system rather than a standalone tool
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under Horizontal's maintenance. Tella's use in human-rights documentation is documented by the organisation; I verified no specific deployment.
assessment: Adopt it where you work with field documenters or stringers in hostile environments — the combination of encrypted capture, camouflage and upload to your own infrastructure has no real alternative. For your profile two things must accompany deployment: an honest briefing that camouflage delays discovery rather than preventing it, and a receiving server you actually operate, because the app's value depends on evidence getting off the device and into a collection you control.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Horizontal's institutional maintenance, with ongoing development on the Android client. Maintenance assessed on activity and institutional backing; release cadence was not separately itemised in this survey.
licence: GPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
licence_restrictions: Copyleft on the application; immaterial for deployment, relevant if you fork it for a bespoke build.
costs: Free. You need a receiving server or Uwazi instance — the real cost, and one you may already have. Estimate.
privacy: Encrypted local storage, camouflage, and upload only to infrastructure you specify — a strong posture designed for exactly this threat. Residual risks are physical: device search by a trained searcher, and the incriminating presence of the app itself.
alternatives: ProofMode for capture provenance without the camouflage and secure-storage features
Signal for sending material to a journalist directly, with no local encryption at rest
A clean device with immediate upload and deletion, where connectivity allows
blockers: Camouflage delays rather than prevents discovery; app presence may itself be incriminating
summary: Mobile application for documenting human-rights violations and collecting evidence in hostile environments…

name: Ushahidi Platform
purpose: Platform for collecting, verifying and mapping crowdsourced reports from SMS, email, web forms and social media, with workflow for review and categorisation and a map-based public view.
journalism_use_case: Running a public reporting channel around an unfolding event: election irregularities, protest incidents, service failures — collected from the public via multiple channels, triaged by a desk, and mapped. It is the established tool for turning distributed observation into a reviewable dataset.
pros: Multi-channel intake including SMS is the distinguishing capability and matters enormously where smartphone penetration or connectivity is limited — a reporting channel that works on a feature phone
Built-in verification workflow means crowdsourced reports are triaged rather than published raw, which is the difference between journalism and a rumour map
Long institutional history with deployments across many elections and crises, so the model is proven and the pitfalls are documented
Open source and self-hostable, so reports and reporter identities stay under your control
cons: Crowdsourced reports are unverified by nature, and the platform's map view makes them look authoritative — the editorial discipline around publication matters more than the software, and this is where deployments fail
Operational commitment: a PHP/API platform plus SMS gateway integration, and the SMS channel in particular has real per-message costs and telecom relationships

Submitter safety is a serious consideration: a public reporting channel in a repressive environment collects identifying information about people reporting on their government, and that database becomes a target
Development pace has moderated relative to the platform's peak years, so check liveness before a time-critical deployment
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under Ushahidi's maintenance. The platform's election and crisis deployments are extensively documented publicly, which is strong evidence that the model works at scale.
assessment: Pilot it for a defined event where public reporting adds something a newsroom cannot gather itself — elections are the canonical case. For your profile the two decisions that matter are editorial and security, not technical: publish only triaged reports and label verification status visibly, and treat the submitter database as source material requiring the same protection, because in a repressive context a list of people who reported on the state is exactly what an adversary wants. Budget SMS costs explicitly.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Ushahidi's institutional maintenance, with moderated development activity compared with the platform's earlier years. Classified stable-low: a mature platform with continuing institutional backing rather than active feature development.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Submitted reports are user-contributed content whose handling is your responsibility as data controller.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-family copyleft would apply to a modified hosted instance. The weightier obligations are data-protection ones arising from collecting reports from identifiable members of the public.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure plus — significantly — SMS gateway costs, which are per-message and can be substantial at scale during an event (rates vary by country and provider; not priced here). Staff cost for triage is the other major item. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps reports and submitter details under your control, which is essential. The database is highly sensitive: it identifies people who reported on events, often adversely to their government, and should be treated with source-protection discipline including minimal retention.
alternatives: A simple form plus a spreadsheet for a small, short event
Tella for documentation by trained contributors rather than open crowdsourcing
Atlos for verification workflow over media rather than open report intake
blockers: Submitter database is a high-value target in repressive environments; SMS channel has real per-message costs
summary: Platform for collecting, verifying and mapping crowdsourced reports from SMS, email, web forms and social media…
additional_costs_note: mandatory per-message SMS gateway charges for the SMS channel (rates vary by country, not priced); self-hosted infrastructure; staff triage effort
